en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on the Indeterminate Rules (Aniyatakaṇḍa)
1. The First Aniyata Training Rule Venerable sirs, these two undetermined rules (aniyata-dhamma) come up for recitation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Udāyī was a frequent visitor to families in Sāvatthī and would approach many households.
On one occasion, a young girl from the family of the Venerable Udāyī’s supporters had been given in marriage to a young man of another family.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Udāyī dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to that family. Having arrived, he asked the people there:
“Where is so-and-so? They replied,
“Venerable sir, she has been given to a young man of such-and-such a family.”
That family was also a supporter of the Venerable Udāyī.
Then the Venerable Udāyī went to that family and, having arrived, asked the people, "Where is so-and-so?"
They said to him, “Venerable sir, she is sitting in the inner room.
Then the Venerable Udāyī approached that young girl; having approached, he [addressed] that young girl...
He sat down alone with her in private on a secluded seat suitable for intimacy, conversing at appropriate times and speaking of the Dhamma at appropriate times.
Now at that time, Visākhā Migāramātā had many sons and many grandsons; her sons and grandsons were healthy, and she was highly esteemed as auspicious.
At sacrifices, festivals, and celebrations, people would feed Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, first.
On one occasion, having been invited, Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, went to that family.
There she saw the Venerable Udāyī sitting alone with her daughter on a secluded seat, suitable for intimacy.
Having seen him, he said this to the Venerable Udāyī:
“Venerable sir, it is neither fitting nor proper that the Master should sit alone with a woman on a secluded seat, one that is private and conducive to intimacy.
Although, venerable sir, the Master has no interest in that matter, nevertheless people who lack faith are difficult to convince.”
Even though he was addressed in this way by Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, the Venerable Udāyī did not heed her.
Then Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, went out and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [as before] ...were indignant, disparaged him, and complained, saying:
“How indeed could the Venerable Udāyī sit down alone with a woman on a secluded, concealed seat suitable for sexual intercourse?
Then those monks, having rebuked the Venerable Udāyī in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, Udāyī, that you sat down alone with a woman on a secluded, concealed seat suitable for sexual intercourse?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:

“… How can you, foolish man, sit down alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed seat that is suitable for sexual intercourse? This will not lead to the welfare of the many, nor to the happiness of the many, nor to compassion for the world, nor for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of devas and humans. Having rebuked him, the Blessed One gave a teaching on the Dhamma and addressed the monks: “Monks, if a monk sits down alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed seat that is suitable for sexual intercourse, he commits an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa).”
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without faith...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘If any monk should sit down alone with a woman on a secluded seat suitable for misconduct, and a female lay follower whose word is trustworthy should see him...’”

If he should speak of one of three categories of offenses—either a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya*—then a monk who admits to having sat [with a woman] shall be dealt with according to one of those three categories: either a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya*.
Or else, that monk shall be dealt with according to whatever a trustworthy female lay follower (*upāsikā*) may say.
“This is an undetermined rule (aniyata).
As for “whoever,” whoever of such a kind... [and so forth].
"Bhikkhu" ...
[as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Woman" (mātugāma) means:
A human woman, not a female spirit (yakkhī), not a female ghost (petī), and not a female animal; even one born on that very day, let alone one who is older.
"Together" means on one side.
"Alone with one" means there is both a monk and a woman.
"In secret" means:
The seclusion of the eye, the seclusion of the ear.
"Seclusion of the eye" means that it is not possible to see [the object] while the eye is being rubbed, or while the eyebrows are being raised, or while the head is being lifted up.
"Secrecy of the ear" means it is not possible to hear ordinary conversation;
"concealed" means...
The seat is concealed by a wall, or a door-panel, or a mat, or a screen-wall, or a tree, or a pillar, or a granary, or by anything whatsoever.
It is "suitable for decoration" means it is possible to engage in sexual intercourse there.
"He should sit down" means:
when a woman is seated, the bhikkhu sits down near her or lies down near her;
or, when the bhikkhu is seated, the woman sits down near him or lies down near him.
Both may be sitting, or both may be lying down. One whose word is trustworthy is called one who has attained the fruit,
one who has realized it, and one who has understood the teaching.
A female lay follower (*upāsikā*) is one who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.
"Having seen" means:
Having seen him, he should charge him with one of three offenses: either a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya*.
If the monk admits to having sat down, he should be dealt with according to one of those three offenses: either a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya*.
Or that monk should be dealt with according to what that trustworthy female lay follower says.
If she should say:
"I have seen the venerable one sitting and engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman," [then he is to be dealt with accordingly].
If he admits that, he should be dealt with according to the offense.
If she should say,
"I saw the venerable one sitting and engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman," [he should be dealt with accordingly].
If he should say,
"It is true that I sat down, but I did not engage in sexual intercourse," he is to be dealt with for the offense of sitting down.
If she should say,
"I have seen the venerable one sitting and engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman," and he should say:
“I am not sitting, but rather lying down,” she should be made to lie down.
If she should say this:
“Venerable sir, I saw you sitting and engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman.
If he should say, “I was not sitting;
rather, I was standing,” [he is to be dealt with according to the rule].
He should not be made to do so.
If she should say,
"I have seen the venerable one lying down, engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman," [he should be dealt with accordingly].
If he admits it, he should be dealt with according to the offense.
If she should say,
"Venerable sir, I saw you lying down, engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman," [he should be dealt with according to the offense].
If he should say,
"It is true that I lay down, but I did not engage in sexual intercourse," he is to be dealt with for the act of lying down.
If she should say,
"I have seen the venerable one lying down engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman," and he should say:
“I am not lying down; rather, I am sitting,” he should be made to sit.
If she should say this:
“If [someone] were to say, ‘I saw the venerable one lying down, engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman,’ and he were to reply,
‘I was not lying down; rather, I was standing’— ”
He should not be made to do so.
If she should say,
"I have seen the venerable one sitting with a woman, engaging in physical contact," [he should be dealt with accordingly].
If he admits that, he should be dealt with according to the offense...
[and so on]... "Truly, I sat down, but I did not engage in physical contact," he should be dealt with according to the offense of sitting down... [and so on].
“I am not sitting, but rather lying down,” he should be made to lie down …pe… “I am not sitting,
but rather standing,” he should be made to stand.
He should not be made to do so.
But if she should say,
"I have seen the venerable one lying down, engaging in physical contact with a woman," [he should be dealt with accordingly].
If he admits it, he is to be dealt with according to the offense... [etc.
... "Truly I lay down, but I did not engage in physical contact," he is to be dealt with for the act of lying down... [etc. ...
“I am not lying down, but rather sitting,” he should be made to sit …pe… “I am not lying down,
but rather standing,” [he should be made to stand].
He should not be made to do so.
If she should say,
"I have seen the venerable one sitting alone with a woman in private, in a secluded seat suitable for misconduct," [he should be dealt with accordingly].
If he admits that, he should be made to undergo the penalty for sitting down...
[and so on] ...if he says, "I was not sitting, but rather lying down," he should be made to undergo the penalty for lying down... [and so on].
If she says, “I am not sitting, but rather standing,” she is not to be made to pay it.
If she should say this:
“If [a monk says], ‘Venerable sir, I saw you alone with a woman, lying down on a secluded and private seat suitable for sexual intercourse,’ and he admits it,
he is to be dealt with according to the offense of lying down … [if he says],
‘I was not lying down, but rather sitting’— ”
He should be made to perform [the offense] while sitting …pe… if he says,
“I am not lying down, but rather standing,” he should not be made to perform it.
"Indeterminate" means it is not fixed as either a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya*.
He confesses to the going, he confesses to the sitting, and he confesses to the offense; he is to be dealt with according to the offense.
If he admits to walking but does not admit to sitting, and admits to an offense, he should be dealt with according to the offense.
If he admits to walking and admits to sitting, but does not admit to an offense, he should be dealt with according to the sitting.
If he admits to walking, does not admit to sitting, and does not admit to an offense, he is not to be dealt with.
If he does not acknowledge the going, but acknowledges the sitting, and acknowledges the offense, he should be dealt with according to the offense.
If he does not acknowledge the going, does not acknowledge the sitting, but acknowledges the offense, he should be dealt with according to the offense.
If he does not acknowledge the going, acknowledges the sitting, but does not acknowledge the offense, he should be dealt with according to the sitting.
He does not acknowledge going; he does not acknowledge sitting; he does not acknowledge the offense; he is not to be dealt with.
The first undetermined rule is finished.
